title: Sh-M-A
hookLine: shema: hear, understand, obey, all at once

cards: "Did you hear me?" A parent in a kitchen asks it, and the kid nods. Yes.
Ten minutes later the shoes are still in the hallway. So did they hear? Their ears did.
In English we'd sort out what went wrong with three verbs: they heard, but didn't really listen, or they listened and didn't obey. Hebrew can do all of that with one root.
Ten days ago you read it letter by letter, as the first word of the Shema. Today, what it means.

teach.b: Sh-M-A. Shin, mem, ayin. Turn it four ways.
First, hear. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The verse opens with a call to the ear: shema.
At the Tower of Babel, God confuses the builders' language, "that they may not understand one another's speech." The verb behind understand comes from this same root.
The builders could still hear each other's voices; they just couldn't take in what was said. Third, obey.

When Abraham is told that all the nations will be blessed through his descendants, the reason given is "because thou hast obeyed my voice." Obeyed is the same root again. Literally: you heard my voice.

teach.h: WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.
teach.b: When the covenant is read to the people, they answer with two verbs: na'aseh v'nishma, we will do, and we will hear.
Some teachers notice the order. Doing comes first and hearing after, as if some things can only be understood by doing them.

Put the four together and the Shema's first word asks for all of it at once: let it in, get it, and let it change what you do. In this root, hearing that changes nothing hasn't quite finished hearing.

how: Jews say the Shema in the evening and morning prayers and at bedtime, and it is customary to cover the eyes with the right hand while saying its first line.

o: one root for hear, understand and obey
a root that means to see and to watch
a root that means to speak or call out

games.q: one root, three meanings — tap the pairs.
p: we will do, and we will hear

s: in Hebrew, hear and obey come from different roots
"thou hast obeyed my voice" uses the same root as shema: you heard my voice.
at Sinai, the people say "we will do" before "we will hear"
na'aseh v'nishma. some teachers make a lesson of the order.
they could still hear. the root says they could not understand.

games.q: the covenant has just been read aloud to the whole people at Sinai. you're in the crowd. what do they answer?
o: "we will hear it, and then decide."
"we will do, and we will hear."
games.why: na'aseh v'nishma: doing comes first in their answer. some teachers read it as trust that understanding comes through doing.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable and start with the nearest sound, your own breath, then widen: the room, something humming, a car, a voice through a wall.

Let each one all the way in without naming or judging it, and when a thought starts to answer or plan, come back to the hearing. If you pray, you can say the first two words, Shema Yisrael, and then stop, and listen.

wordCard.voice: Sh-M-A. Shin, mem, ayin: to hear, to understand, to obey, all in one root. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: he heard; the root shin, mem, ayin covers hearing, understanding and obeying.

carryVoice: Your line: to hear is to heed. The ears are only where it starts. Same time tomorrow.
